summary: Leaving the synagogue, Jesus enters Simon’s house, takes his feverish mother-in-law by the hand, and she rises at once and serves them.
key_insight: A high fever leaves a person weak for days. Simon’s mother-in-law got up immediately and served them. Jesus did not only break the fever; He gave back her strength in the same moment.
story: As soon as they came out of the synagogue in Capernaum, Jesus went with James and John to the house of Simon and Andrew. {Mk}
Simon’s wife’s mother was lying sick with a high fever, {Lk} and they told Jesus about her at once. {Mk}
Jesus stood over her and rebuked the fever. {Lk} He took her by the hand and lifted her up, {Mk} and the fever left her. Immediately she got up and served them.
differences: Only Mark says James and John came along and that the house belonged to Simon and Andrew.
Luke calls it a high fever and says Jesus “rebuked the fever.” Mark says He took her by the hand and lifted her up; Matthew says He touched her hand.
In Mark and Luke, others tell Jesus about her; in Matthew, Jesus sees her Himself.
Mark and Luke place the healing right after the synagogue in Capernaum. Matthew tells it later in his book, after the Sermon on the Mount, with other healings.

scene.label: Peter’s house
scene.text: Under the remains of a fifth-century church in Capernaum, archaeologists found a first-century house whose main room was later plastered and used for Christian gatherings, with Christian graffiti scratched into the walls. Many think it was Peter’s house. That cannot be proved, but early Christians clearly honored it.

scene.label: A married apostle
scene.text: Peter had a wife. Years later Paul mentions that Cephas took along “a believing wife” on his travels (1 Corinthians 9:5). Families often shared one house, and Peter’s mother-in-law was part of that household.

scene.label: Fever
scene.text: Fevers, likely including malaria, were common around the lake, and with no medicine to bring them down they could kill. Luke, whom Paul calls “the beloved physician” (Colossians 4:14), uses the term for a high or severe fever.

scene.label: A Sabbath meal
scene.text: This was still the Sabbath. The main Sabbath meal was usually eaten after the morning synagogue service, with food prepared the day before. Her serving probably means she took her place as hostess at that meal.

witnesses.matthew: Groups this healing with the leper and the centurion’s servant (Matthew 8:1–15): a leper, a Gentile and a woman, three people the religious world of the day held at a distance, each restored by Jesus. Matthew alone says Jesus saw her first and touched her hand.
witnesses.mark: Tells it as the next step in one long Sabbath day: synagogue, house, then the crowd at sunset. Mark names who was there, Simon and Andrew with James and John, and says Jesus “took her by the hand and lifted her up.”
witnesses.luke: Uses a physician’s language, “a high fever,” and says Jesus “rebuked the fever,” the same word he used for the demon a few verses earlier (Luke 4:35). In Luke, sickness and evil spirits alike answer to Jesus’ word.

seeing.reveals: Jesus brings the authority He showed in the synagogue into an ordinary home. The Lord who silenced a demon in public bends over one sick woman in private and restores her completely.
seeing.living: The disciples’ first move was simple: “they told Him about her at once.” Bring the needs of your own household to Jesus as plainly as they did. And when He raises you up, use the strength He gives to serve.
seeing.ponder: Whose need in your own home have you not yet told Jesus about?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus brings His power home, and those He raises up rise to serve.
outline: Friends tell Him of a need (30)
preaching.watch_for: Mark’s word for “served” is the word Jesus later uses for His own mission: the Son of Man did not come “to be served, but to serve” (Mark 10:45). The first sick person Jesus heals in Mark’s Gospel responds by doing what He came to do.
